kw: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
lede: A samurai fireman's orphaned son who turned the rain, snow, moonlight and crowded roads of old Japan into cheap woodblock prints, and whose views of Edo, thirty years after his death, taught Van Gogh and the Impressionists a new way to see.

ps: Utagawa Hiroshige was born in Edo, today's Tokyo, in 1797, as Ando Tokutaro. He became the great master of the landscape print in the last decades of Japan's long isolation.
His series The Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido (1833 to 1834) showed travellers on the highway between Edo and Kyoto in every weather and season. It made him famous and was reprinted for decades.
In his last years he made One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, a series of bold, upright views of his home city. He died in a cholera epidemic in Edo in 1858, aged about 61.
His father, Ando Gen'emon, was a low-ranking samurai in the shogun's fire brigade, living in the fire station barracks near Edo Castle. The family was respectable but not rich.
In 1809, when the boy was twelve, both his mother and his father died. He inherited his father's post as a fire warden, which brought a small fixed income.

ps.t: Around 1811 he became a pupil of the print designer Utagawa Toyohiro, after first trying for a place with the more famous Utagawa Toyokuni, who had no room for him.
ps.why: The story of the refusal comes from later accounts; his apprenticeship to Toyohiro is certain.

ps: By 1812 he had been given the art name Hiroshige. For years he designed ordinary prints of actors, beautiful women and warriors, while also studying the Kano school of painting and Western ideas of perspective seen in imported pictures. In 1823 he handed the fire warden post to a relative.
1831. His series Famous Places in the Eastern Capital showed that his real gift was landscape.

ps.t: 1832. He is said to have travelled along the Tokaido highway with an official party taking horses as a gift from the shogun to the emperor in Kyoto, sketching as he went.
ps.why: The journey is a traditional story with no firm record. Some of his views follow earlier printed guidebooks closely.

ps: 1833 to 1834. The publisher Hoeido brought out The Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido: 55 prints, one for each post town plus the start at Nihonbashi in Edo and the end in Kyoto. It was a huge hit. Over his career he designed around twenty more Tokaido series.
1835 to 1838. He shared The Sixty-nine Stations of the Kisokaido, the inland highway, with the artist Keisai Eisen, and completed it after Eisen dropped out.
1841 to 1843. The shogun's Tempo reforms banned luxury and restricted prints of actors and courtesans. Landscapes, birds and flowers were safe subjects, and his work flourished.
1856. He took Buddhist vows and began One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, published by Uoya Eikichi. The series grew to 118 prints.

1858. A cholera epidemic killed tens of thousands in Edo. Hiroshige died on 12 October and was buried at the temple of Togakuji in Asakusa. His pupil Shigenobu, who married his adopted daughter, took the name Hiroshige II.

Ukiyo-e prints were made by teams. The artist drew the design, a carver cut it into cherry-wood blocks, one for each colour, and a printer pressed them onto paper by hand. A print cost roughly the price of a bowl of noodles.

The Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido. Famous sheets include Night Snow at Kambara, a silent village under snow, and Shono, where travellers and porters run bent against a sudden shower slanting across the picture.

One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. He often put something huge and close in the foreground, a branch, a horse's leg, a lantern, and set the view far behind it. In Plum Park in Kameido (1857) the dark trunk of an old plum tree crosses the whole sheet, with blossoms and tiny strollers beyond.
Sudden Shower over Shin-Ohashi Bridge and Atake (1857), with fine lines of rain falling on people hurrying over a bridge, is one of the most admired prints ever made.
He also designed thousands of other prints, including birds and flowers, fan prints and illustrated books. His deep blues, often from imported Prussian blue pigment, became his trademark.
Utagawa Toyohiro (1773 to 1828), his teacher, a quiet master of gentle landscapes.

Katsushika Hokusai (1760 to 1849), the older genius whose Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (about 1830 to 1832) opened the market for landscape prints. Hiroshige later made his own Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.
Keisai Eisen (1790 to 1848), his partner on the Kisokaido series.
Takenouchi Magohachi of Hoeido and Uoya Eikichi, the publishers who backed his two greatest series.
Vincent van Gogh (1853 to 1890), who never met him but in Paris in 1887 copied Plum Park in Kameido and Sudden Shower in oil paint.

Edo was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps a million people. Peace under the Tokugawa shoguns had lasted two centuries, and roads like the Tokaido were busy with lords, merchants and pilgrims.
Ordinary people could not easily travel abroad, or always even at home. Prints of famous places worked as souvenirs and armchair travel.

In 1853, five years before his death, Commodore Perry's American warships arrived off Edo and forced Japan to open its ports. In 1855 a great earthquake struck the city, and many scholars read the Hundred Views as a celebration of Edo rebuilt.
After Japan opened, prints flowed to Europe, at first sometimes as packing material. In Paris they set off a craze called Japonisme.
Van Gogh collected hundreds of Japanese prints. Claude Monet hung Hiroshige's prints in his house at Giverny, and James McNeill Whistler's misty Thames nocturnes owe much to them.
Complete sets of the Hundred Views survive in museums such as the Brooklyn Museum. His prints are among the best-known images of Japan in the world.

myths.c: Hiroshige and Hokusai were bitter rivals.
myths.t: They competed in the same market for landscape prints, but there is no good evidence of a personal feud. Hokusai was 37 years older and his style was very different.

myths.c: He sketched every Tokaido scene on the road.
myths.t: He may have travelled the highway in 1832, but no record proves it, and several prints borrow their layouts from earlier guidebook illustrations.
In 1887 he painted versions of Plum Park in Kameido and Sudden Shower over Shin-Ohashi, adding bright borders with Japanese characters. Both are in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.
The Great Wave off Kanagawa is by Hokusai, from his Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.
